# How Yammu found its canonical form

The ASCII form *yammu* is not missing anything ​that this name requires. **Yammu** is the canonical spelling supported by the Phoenician evidence and the tradition's scholarly conventions. This post explains what that form preserves, how it ‌is pronounced, which narratives surround it, and why consistency matters. There are no recovered accents to celebrate; there is something more useful — a spelling whose history can ‌actually be checked.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Yammu
- **ASCII form:** yammu
- **Meaning:** "Sea"
- **Domain of influence:** Sea, Chaos
- **Pantheon:** Phoenician
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𐤉𐤌 (Phoenician)

## ​Overview

**Yammu** (*yammu*) — The Sea, Rival of Baʿal · Sea — belongs to the Phoenician tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Sea, Chaos". The name means ​"Sea".

**Yammu** is the Canaanite sea-god: the personified ocean whose rebellion against the divine council set the Baal Cycle in motion, and whose defeat by Baʿal — with ​two magic clubs thrown from the storm-cloud — established the storm-god’s kingship over the gods. The Ugaritic tablets of the fourteenth century BCE, found in 1929, gave him ​back his name after three thousand years of silence.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **Yammu** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/yammu/). The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — ​a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *yammu* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here ‌is consistent citation, capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Name

The name is attested in Phoenician as **𐤉𐤌**. Etymologically it means "Sea".

The canonical spelling **Yammu** matches the ​conventional scholarly romanization. The plain ASCII form *yammu* contains the same letters, so no lost diacritics or encoding transition is claimed. The editorial work is to fix one ​reviewed reference spelling, preserve capitalization and provenance, and keep the original evidence visible. The displayed form is ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

## ​The Original Script

The name is preserved in Phoenician as **𐤉𐤌** — Phoenician alphabet, attested Phoenician, c. 1050–800 BCE, in Levant / Mediterranean. The script is written right-to-left.

‌The scholarly transliteration is *Yammu* (Phoenician linear alphabet), giving the normalized reading /ˈjam.mu/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Phoenician y-m, the Semitic word for 'sea'
- The doubled ​mm in the absolute state produces Yammu
- Personified Sea in the Baal Cycle

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈjɑːmʊ/** — Ugaritic (conventional vocalisation).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- ‌**Ym** — Written ym in Ugaritic cuneiform; conventionally vocalised “Yammu”. The word means “sea”.
- **** — The Canaanite sea-god, rival and enemy of Baʿal, defeated in the great ​Baal Cycle of Ugarit.
- **** — The name needs no vowels the Ugaritic scribes would not have recognised — a plain transliteration.

For the modern speaker, the closest ​approximation is: “YAH-moo”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Akkadian** — Tiamat’s kin — the sea-monster of the Enūma eliš
- **Rival** — Baal (Baʿlu) — the storm-god of ​the Ugaritic tablets

He is the sea itself as god: the oldest named enemy in the Baal Cycle, defeated at the world’s beginning.

## Mythology

Yammu’s mythology is the ​Baal Cycle’s opening act: the sea demands the storm-god’s surrender, the council wavers, and Baʿal — armed by the craftsman-god Kothar-wa-Khasis with two magic clubs — goes out ​to meet the flood and splits the sea’s skull between the eyes. It is the Levant’s own dragon-combat — the same pattern as Marduk and Tiamat, Indra and ‌Vritra, told in the oldest alphabetic literature on earth.

### The Embassy of the Sea (KTU 1.2)

The cycle opens with Yammu’s envoys at the divine council, demanding that Baʿal ​be delivered into the sea’s power. El, the aged king of the gods, wavers — and it is left to Baʿal himself, with Kothar-wa-Khasis’s weapons, to answer the ‌demand. The scene sets the cycle’s whole theology: kingship is taken, not granted.

### The Two Magic Clubs (KTU 1.2 iv)

Kothar-wa-Khasis gives Baʿal two clubs — Yaggarish, “Chaser”, ​and Ayyamarri, “Driver”. Baʿal strikes Yammu between the eyes, on the skull: ‘Yammu is dead! Baʿal is king!’ The lines are the Levantine storm-god’s coronation — and the ‌pattern that Hebrew poetry would echo in its own sea-combat, Yahweh versus Yam.

### Yam in the Psalms (Biblical Echoes)

The Hebrew Bible keeps the sea-god’s name as a common ​noun and his defeat as a motif: ‘Thou didst divide the sea (yam) by thy strength’, ‘thou rulest the raging of the sea (yam)’. The Ugaritic tablets revealed ‌what the Psalms were arguing against — and what they preserved: Yammu’s defeat is the Old Testament sea’s backstory.

### The Sea-Enemy Pattern (Comparative Frame)

Yammu belongs to the ​oldest myth-complex in the lexicon: the storm-god versus the sea. Tiamat and Marduk in Babylon, Vritra and Indra in the Rigveda, Typhon and Zeus in Greece — the pattern ‌crosses the whole ancient world, and the Ugaritic telling is among its most vivid witnesses. The sea is always first, and always beaten.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography ​associated with Yammu concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Sea Itself** — His name IS the word “sea” ​(ym) — the ocean as the first rebel against order.
- **The Two Clubs** — “Chaser” and “Driver”, the magic clubs Baʿal threw to shatter his skull — the ‌cycle’s most quoted scene.
- **The Divine Council** — He demanded Baʿal’s surrender from the council of El; the gods’ cowardice set the war in motion.
- **The Tablet’s Return** — ‌Found at Ugarit (Ras Shamra) in 1929 — the Baal Cycle restored Canaanite religion to history.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Yammu survives in a small ‌number of securely identified remains, catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Yammu’s monuments are the ​tablets: the Baal Cycle’s cuneiform pages from Ras Shamrt (Ugarit), 1929 — the oldest large alphabetic texts ever found, and the foundation-stones of Northwest Semitic philology.

## Across Cultures

Yammu is the Canaanite branch of the ancient Near Eastern sea-enemy — Tiamat’s cousin, with the Babylonian goddess-dragon as his nearest kin. The Hebrew ​tradition suppressed him into a noun but kept his combat; and modern study of the Baal Cycle restored him as the indispensable witness to what Israel’s religion argued ‌with. The Greeks of the coast heard Poseidon in him; the scholars hear the pattern.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[angrboda|Angrboða]] (chaos / primordial / world ​serpent), [[apep|ꜥꜣpp]] (chaos / primordial / world serpent), [[aseratu|Ašeratu]] (sea / water), [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]] (sea / water), [[benzaiten|Benzaiten]] (sea / water), and [[chaos|Cháos]] (chaos / primordial / world serpent).

## ‌Cultural Legacy

The Baal Cycle’s discovery in 1929 rewrote the history of Canaanite and biblical religion — Yammu’s defeat gave the Psalms their sea-imagery’s original. In Ugaritic studies ​his name heads every syllabus; and the sea-monster pattern he anchors remains the comparative mythologist’s oldest exhibit.
